title: Is the first idli-vada number always the lowest common multiple?
description: The first idli-vada number is found for fourteen and thirty, and then for fifteen and fifty five, using the lists of multiples. The lists show it is always the lowest common multiple. Keeko doubts this and wants to multiply fourteen and thirty, which gives a number twice as big as the first.
teaching_notes: One idea: the first number found in both lists of multiples is by its meaning the lowest common multiple. Watch for students who multiply the two numbers and call the product the first, when half of it already works.

source: Find the first number for which idli-vada will be called out, for 14 and 30, and for 15 and 55. Is the answer always the LCM of the two numbers?
video_script.why: The child has found the first idli-vada number for small pairs and now meets larger pairs where the lists are long, and asks whether the first number is always the lowest common multiple.
video_script.substitution: List the multiples of each number, take the first number in both lists, and read it as the lowest common multiple.
video_script.anchor: Two rows of multiples written one under the other for each pair, with the idli row and the vada row labelled.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies fourteen and thirty to get four hundred twenty, but half of it, two hundred ten, already gets both calls.
video_script.payoff_line: The first idli-vada numbers are two hundred ten and one hundred sixty five

final_answer.spoken: two hundred ten and one hundred sixty five

never_show: 420 as the first idli-vada number, marked right
maths_rules: multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, 120, 135, 150, 165; multiples of 55: 55, 110, 165; the first number in both is 165
the first number in both lists is by definition the lowest common multiple, so yes, always
slip: 14 × 30 = 420 is in both lists, but 420 ÷ 2 = 210 is in both lists too and comes first
video_script.design: One idea: the first number in both lists of multiples is the lowest common multiple, by its meaning. The long lists are shown in full on the board and only a few terms are spoken.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>In the idli-vada game, find the first idli-vada number. Take fourteen and thirty, and then fifteen and fifty five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The lowest of all the common multiples of two numbers is called their lowest common multiple. Is the first idli-vada number always that one?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, take fourteen and thirty. The multiples of fourteen are fourteen, twenty eight, forty two, and on up to two hundred ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The multiples of thirty are thirty, sixty, ninety, one hundred twenty. Then come one hundred fifty, one hundred eighty, two hundred ten.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The first number in both lists is two hundred ten.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, take fifteen and fifty five. The multiples of fifteen run from fifteen, thirty, forty five, up to one hundred sixty five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The multiples of fifty five are fifty five, one hundred ten, one hundred sixty five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The first number in both lists is one hundred sixty five.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the first number in both lists is the lowest of the common multiples.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That is the meaning of lowest common multiple, so the answer is yes, always.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The first idli-vada numbers are two hundred ten and one hundred sixty five. And yes, it is always the lowest common multiple.
